summary:
This project aims to create an interactive digital storytelling platform that explores the history and legacy of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars during space exploration missions. From lunar landers and rovers to scientific instruments, parachutes, heat shields, and other mission hardware, these objects represent important milestones in humanity's journey into space.

Although these objects are no longer operational or have been abandoned after completing their missions, they remain valuable historical and scientific artifacts. The project will use NASA's Open Science Data, mission photographs, maps, videos, and publicly available information to document where these objects are located, why they were left behind, and what stories they tell about space exploration.

Expected Outcome
The expected outcome is an educational, interactive digital platform that preserves the stories of NASA's space exploration hardware. It will help school students, teachers, and space enthusiasts understand how these machines contributed to scientific discoveries and expanded humanity's knowledge of the Moon and Mars.

The project will demonstrate that even equipment left behind after a mission can continue to contribute to science, education, and future exploration.
details:
Project Objectives

  1. Identify and document NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars.
  2. Explain the purpose and scientific objectives of each mission.
  3. Show the original landing photographs alongside modern orbital images.
  4. Describe why the equipment was left behind and its present condition.
  5. Explain the scientific discoveries made possible by the equipment.
  6. Develop an interactive educational experience for students.
  7. Promote the use of open NASA scientific data for learning and exploration.

4. Proposed Hardware and Mission Stories

The PowerPoint identifies six important examples of NASA equipment to feature in the storytelling platform.

Far above the Earth, NASA's Apollo lunar lander put astronauts on the moon

1. Apollo 11 – Tranquility Base

1969

  • Lunar Module descent stage and laser reflector remain on the Moon.
  • Story: Humanity's first crewed Moon landing.
  • Science: Lunar laser ranging and precision measurements of the Earth–Moon system.

Long History and Bright Future of Space Sample Deliveries - NASA Science

2. Surveyor 3 and Apollo 12

1969

  • Apollo 12 astronauts visited Surveyor 3.
  • Some components were brought back to Earth for examination.
  • Story: A human mission revisits a robotic spacecraft and studies its exposure to the lunar environment.

3. Lunar Roving Vehicles

1971–1972

  • Used during Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
  • Enabled astronauts to travel farther across the lunar surface.
  • Story: How electric mobility expanded lunar exploration.

View of the Central Station of the ALSEP deploy by Apollo 14 astronauts - PICRYL - Public Domain Media Search Engine Public Domain Search

4. Apollo ALSEP Science Stations

1969–1977

  • Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages.
  • Scientific instruments collected lunar data until 1977.
  • Story: How abandoned scientific stations continued transmitting information about the Moon.

Missing Piece Inspires New Look at Mars Puzzle | NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)

5. Viking 1 Mars Lander

1976–1982

  • One of NASA's first successful long-duration Mars landers.
  • Conducted experiments and studied the Martian environment.
  • Story: Early robotic exploration and the search for evidence of life on Mars.

6. Opportunity Mars Rover

2004–2019

  • Designed for a 90-day mission but operated for approximately 15 years.
  • Explored Martian rocks, soil and evidence of ancient water.
  • Story: A remarkable engineering achievement and an unexpectedly long scientific journey.

Note: Mission dates and equipment details should be checked against NASA's original mission records before publication.

NASA_SpaceApps_Discarded_Equipment.pptx

5. Storytelling Methodology – Four Stages

Every piece of equipment will have its own digital story organized into four stages.

  1. Launch – Why NASA sent it
    Explain the mission objectives, engineering design, launch vehicle and scientific questions.
  2. Landing – The moment it reached the surface
    Present landing photographs, location, landing date and mission milestones.
  3. Left Behind – Why it stayed
    Explain why the hardware remained on the planetary surface and show its location through orbital imagery.
  4. Still Teaching – The science it made possible
    Present discoveries, scientific contributions, engineering lessons and relevance to future exploration.

6. NASA Data Sources and Research Methodology

The project will use authentic NASA datasets and scientific archives rather than relying only on secondary descriptions.

Data source

Application

LROC Featured Sites

Orbital images of lunar equipment and landing sites

HiRISE

High-resolution orbital images of Mars

NSSDCA Master Catalog

Mission details and hardware verification

NASA Image Library

Launch, landing and surface photographs

Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

Astronaut mission records

PDS Geosciences Node

Apollo scientific datasets

Research workflow:

  1. Select a hardware object and identify its mission.
  2. Collect mission details from NSSDCA.
  3. Locate its original surface photographs.
  4. Search for modern orbital photographs using LROC or HiRISE.
  5. Verify its operational history and scientific contributions.
  6. Develop a visual story with appropriate NASA image credits.

The presentation specifically highlights NASA's catalogue of man-made material on the Moon, which lists 796 catalogued items.
